\chapter{Evaluation}
\label{ch:results}

Chapter~\ref{ch:setup} fixed what was run: three models, eight scenarios,
three frameworks, one sample per cell. This chapter asks what it shows.
Rather than walking through every cell one at a time, it is organised
around six research questions that each aggregate across every cell,
model, and scenario collected, closing with a synthesis that draws the
six answers together and connects them back to the thesis's central
question (Section~\ref{sec:intro-missing}): \emph{can an LLM agent
iteratively optimise the deployment configuration of a backend application
on a Kubernetes cluster, guided by runtime performance feedback, to
maximise sustainable throughput under fixed infrastructure constraints?}

\textbf{63 of the 72 scenario$\times$framework$\times$model cells in the
evaluated matrix have experiment data.} The nine without data are
concentrated in one scenario: \textsc{TimeCapsuleNotesVault} has data for
only one of its nine possible model$\times$framework combinations
(\texttt{gpt-5.5} on \textsc{Go-net-http}); the remaining gap is one
further \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} cell
(\textsc{BranchWeave}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix}). Every one of the 63
cells with data reached a working baseline deployment and completed the
full ten-iteration refinement budget, for all three models
(Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3}). This chapter therefore treats
\textsc{TimeCapsuleNotesVault} as excluded from scenario-level and
cross-model comparisons rather than as a genuine data point, and flags it
again wherever it would otherwise distort an aggregate.


% ----- §5.1 Overview -----
\section{Overview of the Collected Data}
\label{sec:results-overview}

This chapter reports on \textbf{63 Kubernetes experiments} spanning three
models, \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}, \texttt{gpt-5.5}, and \texttt{glm-5.2},
crossed with the eight scenarios and three frameworks of
Chapter~\ref{ch:setup}, one sample per cell, run under the
\texttt{k8s-explore-refine} load profile with a ten-iteration refinement
budget ($N{=}10$). \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} contributes 20 of its 24
possible cells, \texttt{gpt-5.5} contributes 22, and \texttt{glm-5.2}
contributes 21; Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3} details the nine cells
without data.

All figures and summary statistics are produced by a single aggregation
script (\texttt{scripts/analysis/aggregate\_evaluation.py}), which walks
every experiment tree under \texttt{results/} and tabulates per-iteration
goodput, refinement lever, deployment-spec knobs, and recorded failure
records.
%
\textbf{Caveat on sample size.} Every cell in this chapter is a single
sample (one code-generation seed) run once (Section~\ref{sec:setup-procedure}).
The comparisons below are therefore \emph{descriptive}, not statistically
tested; medians and individual scenario-level points are shown side by
side throughout so the reader can judge dispersion directly rather than
trust a single summary statistic. Section~\ref{sec:discussion-limitations}
returns to what this does and does not license us to claim.


% ----- §5.2 RQ1 -----
\section{RQ1: Does Iterative Refinement Improve Sustained Goodput?}
\label{sec:results-rq1}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=1\linewidth]{figures/eval/goodput_trajectories_grid.pdf}
  \caption{Sustained goodput per iteration, one panel per scenario$\times$framework
    cell, coloured by model. A missing line for a model means that model
    has no experiment data for that cell; see Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3}.}
  \label{fig:results-trajectories-grid}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{figures/eval/baseline_vs_best_by_model.pdf}
  \caption{Median baseline (iteration \texttt{000}) vs.\ best-refined-iteration
    goodput, per model. Bars show the per-model median across cells; dots show
    every individual scenario$\times$framework cell.}
  \label{fig:results-baseline-vs-best}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evidence.}
Table~\ref{tab:results-rq1-summary} and Figures~\ref{fig:results-trajectories-grid}--\ref{fig:results-baseline-vs-best}
summarise all 63 cells at the model level.

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{Baseline vs.\ best-iteration goodput, by model (median over all
    cells with data; $n$ = number of scenario$\times$framework cells;
    ``healthy'' = baseline goodput $>0$). $n$ is out of a possible 24 per
    model; Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3} accounts for the gap.}
  \label{tab:results-rq1-summary}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrrr@{}}
    \toprule
    \textbf{Model} & $n$ cells & Median baseline & Median best & Baseline $>0$ & Median gain (healthy) \\
    \midrule
    \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} & 20 & 1{,}413.2  & 15{,}495.5 & 11 / 20 & $5.8\times$ \\
    \texttt{gpt-5.5}         & 22 & 10{,}868.3 & 32{,}088.2 & 16 / 22 & $2.3\times$ \\
    \texttt{glm-5.2}         & 21 & 0.0        & 13{,}946.2 & 7 / 21  & $1.8\times$ \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

Restricting to cells where the baseline already reached measurable
goodput, the ratio of best-iteration to baseline goodput is positive for
every model. \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s median healthy-baseline gain is $2.3\times$
over 16 cells (mean $9.5\times$, pulled up by a $75.4\times$ outlier on
\textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http}, where the baseline was
severely under-provisioned at 48 replicas and a full CPU core each, against
a $1.1\times$ floor where the baseline was already close to its achievable
ceiling). \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s median is $5.8\times$ over 11 healthy
cells (mean $6.6\times$), ranging from $1.7\times$ to $16.2\times$.
\texttt{glm-5.2}'s median is the lowest of the three, $1.8\times$ over 7
healthy cells (mean $4.7\times$, range $1.0$--$14.9\times$), with its own
largest gain also on \textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http}
($14.9\times$): the same near-stateless, severely under-provisioned
scenario drives the largest observed gain for both models that show a
large-outlier pattern, which is evidence the effect is a property of the
scenario's baseline provisioning rather than of either model individually.

\paragraph{Refinement also rescues \emph{dead} baselines, almost always.}
In several cells the baseline never reaches a sustained plateau at all:
the adaptive load profile's warm-up step fails its health check and the
explore phase never starts (Section~\ref{sec:methods-load-profile}), so
sustained goodput is recorded as exactly $0$\,req/s even though some
requests were technically served during the failed warm-up window. Across
all three models, \textbf{29 of the 63 cells} start this way, and
\textbf{27 of those 29} recover to a benchmarkable, non-zero deployment
somewhere in their trajectory: all 6 of \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s dead baselines
recover, 13 of \texttt{glm-5.2}'s 14 dead baselines recover, and 8 of
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s 9 dead baselines recover. Two cells never
recover across the full ten-iteration budget: \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s
\textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask} and \texttt{glm-5.2}'s
\textsc{TransitPulseDelayReporter}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http}, the latter
recording exactly $0$\,req/s at every one of its ten iterations despite the
decision stage trying both code and deployment refinement across the
trajectory. This is a qualitatively different contribution than the tuning
gains above: it is the loop converting a \emph{non-functional} deployment
into a \emph{functional} one, not just a faster one, though, as the two
non-recovering cases show, not a guarantee.

\paragraph{Improvement is not perfectly monotonic.}
Individual iterations regularly regress goodput relative to the previous
successful iteration (visible as sawtooth segments in
Figure~\ref{fig:results-trajectories-grid}). Because the framework only
advances the ``latest good'' lineage on \emph{successful} benches
(Section~\ref{sec:methods-outcome}), a regression is not silently
compounded: the next iteration's decision stage sees it in its feedback,
and in most cases observed here the trajectory recovers within one to two
iterations. Section~\ref{sec:results-rq6} details one case where the
recovery takes longer.

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
Iterative refinement improves sustained goodput in essentially every cell
with data, and the size of the multiplicative gain is dominated by how
badly under-provisioned the baseline happened to be (largest for both
models that show it on the same near-stateless scenario), which is closer
to a property of the baseline LLM call and the scenario's workload shape
than of the refinement loop itself. Two cells never recover from a dead
baseline regardless of which lever the decision stage tries, which this
dataset cannot yet attribute to a specific structural cause without
further trajectory-level instrumentation.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
\textbf{Yes, with one caveat.} Refinement improves goodput in every model
whenever a cell has data, and in a large majority of cells (27 of 29) it is
not a marginal improvement but the difference between a non-functional and
a functional deployment. The size of the multiplicative gain is not a fixed
``refinement value-add'' comparable across cells: it tracks how
under-provisioned the baseline was, most sharply on the near-stateless
\textsc{ClickCount} scenario, for the two models where a large outlier
appears at all.


% ----- §5.3 RQ2 -----
\section{RQ2: Which Refinement Lever Contributes More: Code or Deployment?}
\label{sec:results-rq2}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.75\linewidth]{figures/eval/code_vs_spec_delta.pdf}
  \caption{Per-step goodput change (\%) relative to the previous
    \emph{successful} iteration, split by refinement lever. Steps whose
    predecessor had zero sustained goodput are excluded here (their delta
    is undefined as a percentage) and discussed under RQ1/RQ6.}
  \label{fig:results-code-vs-spec}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evidence.}
Across all three models, 279 completed iterations chose \textbf{code}
refinement and 289 chose \textbf{deployment (spec)} refinement.
Table~\ref{tab:results-rq2-summary} and Figure~\ref{fig:results-code-vs-spec}
break the resulting per-step goodput change down by model and lever,
restricted to the 184 code and 244 spec steps whose predecessor iteration
was already serving traffic (so a percentage change is defined).

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{Per-step goodput change (\%) by refinement lever and model
    (excludes steps whose predecessor had zero goodput).}
  \label{tab:results-rq2-summary}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrrrr@{}}
    \toprule
    & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{Code}} & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{Spec}} \\
    \textbf{Model} & $n$ & median & mean & $n$ & median & mean \\
    \midrule
    \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} & 65 & $+1.2\%$ & $+5.6\%$  & 76  & $+3.2\%$ & $+5.7\%$ \\
    \texttt{gpt-5.5}         & 74 & $+6.2\%$ & $+26.5\%$ & 102 & $+1.4\%$ & $+1.4\%$ \\
    \texttt{glm-5.2}         & 45 & $+0.4\%$ & $+7.5\%$  & 66  & $+0.5\%$ & $-10.4\%$ \\
    \midrule
    \textbf{All}             & 184 & $+2.2\%$ & $+14.5\%$ & 244 & $+1.5\%$ & $-0.4\%$ \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Code refinement has a heavier tail; deployment refinement is
smaller on median but ranges from strongly positive to catastrophic
depending on the model.} Pooled across all models, the typical (median)
step is modest for both levers (code $+2.2\%$, spec $+1.5\%$), but the
\emph{mean} is pulled up by a handful of large code-side recoveries,
single-step jumps of up to $+334.9\%$ (\texttt{gpt-5.5}), $+259.5\%$
(\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}), and $+259.7\%$ (\texttt{glm-5.2}), where a code
change fixed a latent correctness or connection-handling bug that no
amount of replica or resource tuning could have addressed. Deployment
refinement's mean is model-dependent in a way code refinement's is not:
positive for \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} ($+5.7\%$) and \texttt{gpt-5.5}
($+1.4\%$), but sharply negative for \texttt{glm-5.2} ($-10.4\%$), pulled
down by spec steps that drive a working deployment to zero goodput
outright (Section~\ref{sec:results-rq6} details one such case).
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s spec mean is the only one of the three models
where deployment refinement's mean \emph{exceeds} code refinement's; with
76 spec and 65 code steps this is not a small sample, and is worth reading
alongside RQ4's finding that \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s achievable ceiling
per framework is otherwise comparable to the other two models, since it
suggests the extra spec-side gain is coming from genuine capacity tuning
rather than from a code-quality gap this lever happens to be compensating
for.

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
This supports the framework's decision to keep code and deployment
refinement mutually exclusive per iteration
(Section~\ref{sec:methods-workflow}): the two levers act on genuinely
different failure classes. Code refinement does more of the heavy lifting
for correctness-adjacent bottlenecks, the same class of bug BaxBench's
original single-container evaluation cannot even observe, since it never
applies load (Section~\ref{sec:rw-benchmarks}); deployment refinement does
comparatively fine-grained capacity tuning once the application is already
sound, at the cost of an occasional complete backfire that is concentrated,
in this dataset, in \texttt{glm-5.2}'s cells rather than spread evenly
across all three models.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
\textbf{Code refinement contributes the largest single-step gains and
carries most of the ``fix a broken deployment'' work; deployment
refinement is smaller on median and, for two of three models, positive on
average, but for \texttt{glm-5.2} it is a net-negative, higher-tail-risk
lever rather than a purely marginal one.} With 66 spec steps behind
\texttt{glm-5.2}'s figure, a net-negative spec mean is unlikely to be pure
noise, though this single-model, single-sample dataset cannot rule out that
it reflects something specific to how this model's decision stage phrases
deployment changes rather than a property of deployment refinement as a
lever in general.


% ----- §5.4 RQ3 -----
\section{RQ3: How Do the Models Compare?}
\label{sec:results-rq3}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.75\linewidth]{figures/eval/completion_funnel.pdf}
  \caption{Run completion status per model, counted over the
    scenario$\times$framework cells that have experiment data.
    \textbf{This figure cannot show the 9 cells with no data at all}
    (accounted for separately below); a bar reaching only 20, 22, or 21 is
    that model's count of cells with data, not its full 24-cell
    allocation. ``Completed full trajectory'' = reached iteration 010.}
  \label{fig:results-completion-funnel}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evidence: cells with data.}
Among cells that have any experiment data, all three models are uniform:
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8} reaches a completed baseline in \textbf{20/20} of
its cells and completes the full trajectory in 20/20; \texttt{gpt-5.5} in
\textbf{22/22} and 22/22; \texttt{glm-5.2} in \textbf{21/21} and 21/21
(Figure~\ref{fig:results-completion-funnel}). Every cell that has data, for
every model, reaches a working baseline and completes its full
ten-iteration refinement budget.

\paragraph{Evidence: the 9 missing cells.} Nine of the 72
scenario$\times$framework$\times$model combinations have no experiment
data. Four are \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s: all three
\textsc{TimeCapsuleNotesVault} frameworks, plus
\textsc{BranchWeave}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix}. Two are \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s:
\textsc{TimeCapsuleNotesVault}$\times$\{\textsc{Python-Flask},
\textsc{Rust-Actix}\}. Three are \texttt{glm-5.2}'s: all three
\textsc{TimeCapsuleNotesVault} frameworks. \textsc{TimeCapsuleNotesVault}
alone accounts for eight of the nine missing cells and has data for only
one of its nine possible model$\times$framework combinations
(\texttt{gpt-5.5} on \textsc{Go-net-http}); no other scenario has more than
one missing cell. This concentration is severe enough that this chapter
treats \textsc{TimeCapsuleNotesVault} as excluded from scenario-level and
cross-model comparisons rather than as a usable data point, and
Section~\ref{sec:discussion-limitations} returns to it as a limitation.

\paragraph{Cost.} Measured LLM spend (Table~\ref{tab:setup-model-cost})
shows \texttt{glm-5.2} roughly an order of magnitude cheaper per cell than
\texttt{gpt-5.5} or \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}, computed directly over the
cells each model has data for.

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
Within the 63 cells that have data, this dataset supports a strong,
uniform statement: every model that reaches baseline code generation
completes its full refinement budget, with no partial trajectories or
mid-run failures of the kind that would indicate a reliability difference.
The nine missing cells are concentrated almost entirely in one scenario
rather than spread across the matrix, so they are better read as a
scenario-coverage gap than as a per-model reliability signal.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
\textbf{This dataset does not support a completion-rate ranking between the
three models}: every model reaches a working baseline and completes its
full refinement budget on 100\% of the cells it has data for. What it does
show is a coverage gap concentrated in
\textsc{TimeCapsuleNotesVault}, which materially limits how much this
scenario can contribute to any cross-model or cross-scenario comparison
elsewhere in this chapter.


% ----- §5.5 RQ4 -----
\section{RQ4: Does Framework/Language Choice Affect Achievable Goodput?}
\label{sec:results-rq4}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{figures/eval/framework_comparison.pdf}
  \caption{Best goodput reached per framework (symlog $y$-axis), split by
    model. Each dot is one scenario cell; the horizontal bar is the
    per-model median for that framework.}
  \label{fig:results-framework-comparison}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evidence.}
\textsc{Python-Flask} trails the other two frameworks for all three models
(medians $10{,}436.2$\,req/s for \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}, $22{,}318.1$ for
\texttt{gpt-5.5}, $12{,}069.6$ for \texttt{glm-5.2}), consistent with the
expected throughput ceiling of a single-process WSGI stack under
\texttt{gunicorn}, even after the agent tunes replica count and
worker/pool sizing. The two compiled frameworks are close to each other for
two of the three models and this dataset now has full, seven-of-seven or
better coverage for both compiled frameworks across all three models
(Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3} explains the one \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}
gap). For \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}, \textsc{Go-net-http} leads clearly
($26{,}125.5$ vs.\ $13{,}414.3$\,req/s median for \textsc{Rust-Actix}); for
\texttt{gpt-5.5}, the same ordering holds ($55{,}037.6$ vs.\ $30{,}978.2$).
For \texttt{glm-5.2}, the two compiled frameworks are effectively tied,
with \textsc{Rust-Actix} marginally ahead ($14{,}351.6$ vs.\ $13{,}946.2$\,req/s,
a 3\% difference), the one case in this dataset where
\textsc{Go-net-http} is not the single highest-median framework.

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
The consistent pattern across all three models is
\textsc{Python-Flask}\ $<$ \{\textsc{Go-net-http}, \textsc{Rust-Actix}\},
i.e.\ an interpreted, single-process stack sets a materially lower ceiling
than either compiled runtime under CPU-bound load. The ordering
\emph{between} the two compiled frameworks is not fixed across models:
\textsc{Go-net-http} is ahead for \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} and
\texttt{gpt-5.5}, but statistically indistinguishable from
\textsc{Rust-Actix} for \texttt{glm-5.2} given a 3\% median gap at
seven cells per framework. Framework sets a ceiling that refinement
operates within rather than around, but that ceiling does not always
resolve the same way between two compiled runtimes.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
\textbf{Framework sets an achievable-goodput ceiling that refinement
operates within, not around}, with \textsc{Python-Flask} clearly behind
both compiled frameworks for every model. The ordering between
\textsc{Go-net-http} and \textsc{Rust-Actix} is model-dependent rather than
universal, and for \texttt{glm-5.2} the two are close enough that this
dataset cannot call a clear winner between them.


% ----- §5.6 RQ5 -----
\section{RQ5: What Deployment Parameters Does the Agent Converge To?}
\label{sec:results-rq5}

\paragraph{Evidence.}
Spec prompts intentionally omit recommended numeric ranges
(Section~\ref{sec:methods-spec}), so any sensible-looking convergence in
\texttt{backend.replicas}, per-pod resource requests, or database
topology is evidence the agent is reading load-test and utilisation
feedback rather than falling back on defaults. The clearest example
remains \texttt{gpt-5.5} on \textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http}
(the $75.4\times$ case from RQ1):

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{Spec-knob trajectory for \texttt{gpt-5.5}, \textsc{ClickCount},
    \textsc{Go-net-http} (selected iterations).}
  \label{tab:results-rq5-clickcount}
  \footnotesize
  \begin{tabular}{@{}rrrrrrr@{}}
    \toprule
    Iter.\ & Lever & Goodput (req/s) & Replicas & CPU req.\ & DB repl.\ & DB max\_conn \\
    \midrule
    000 & baseline & 1{,}285.1  & 48  & 1000m & 3 & 500 \\
    006 & code     & 23{,}670.6 & 48  & 1000m & 3 & 500 \\
    007 & spec     & 23{,}640.9 & 192 & 350m  & 1 & 300 \\
    008 & code     & 90{,}653.8 & 192 & 350m  & 1 & 300 \\
    009 & spec     & 91{,}392.6 & 320 & 250m  & 1 & 500 \\
    010 & code     & 96{,}924.9 & 320 & 250m  & 1 & 500 \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

Between iterations 006 and 010, the agent roughly \emph{sextuples}
replica count (48 $\to$ 320) while \emph{quartering} per-pod CPU request
(1000m $\to$ 250m), trading a few large pods for many small ones, and
drops database replicas from 3 to 1. For a scenario whose endpoints are a
near-stateless counter increment (Section~\ref{sec:setup-scenarios}),
this is the correct qualitative direction: per-request CPU cost is
negligible, so raw horizontal fan-out beats per-pod headroom, and the
extra Postgres read replicas the baseline provisioned were never
load-bearing. \texttt{glm-5.2} shows the same qualitative direction on its
own \textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http} cell, its largest
observed gain in this dataset (RQ1), though a full knob-by-knob trajectory
is not reproduced here.

Not every spec-refinement decision pays off, however:
Section~\ref{sec:results-rq6} gives a case where the stated rationale is
reasonable but the resulting deployment regresses to zero goodput, and RQ2
above shows this is not a one-off for \texttt{glm-5.2}: its spec-refinement
mean is net-negative across 66 steps, not just on this one cell.

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
Where the agent has enough successful iterations to work with, its
\texttt{spec.yaml} trajectory tracks the workload's actual scaling
characteristics rather than converging on generic defaults, which is the
behaviour the constrained-schema design of Section~\ref{sec:methods-design}
was intended to elicit. That the two models with the largest observed
gains (\texttt{gpt-5.5} and \texttt{glm-5.2}) both reach it on the same
scenario, via qualitatively similar knob movements, is stronger evidence
than a single case study that this reflects the workload's actual scaling
shape rather than one model's idiosyncratic behaviour.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
\textbf{The agent converges on workload-appropriate deployment parameters
when given the room to iterate}, corroborated on the same scenario by two
different models, but this chapter reports one detailed trajectory, not a
systematic per-cell audit; RQ6's counter-example, and RQ2's model-level
spec statistics, show this is a tendency, not a guarantee.


% ----- §5.7 RQ6 -----
\section{RQ6: Failure Modes and Case Studies}
\label{sec:results-rq6}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.75\linewidth]{figures/eval/failure_taxonomy.pdf}
  \caption{Recorded \texttt{failure.json} occurrences by phase and kind,
    summed across all three models and all cells with data.}
  \label{fig:results-failure-taxonomy}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evidence.}
Of \textbf{62} recorded failures across all cells with data, \textbf{32}
are \texttt{02-code: functional\_test} failures, split 4 / 13 / 15 across
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8} / \texttt{gpt-5.5} / \texttt{glm-5.2}, and these
remain the dataset's largest genuine code-correctness signal.
\textbf{14} are \texttt{docker\_build} failures (Rust or Go code that fails
to compile), 12 of them \texttt{glm-5.2}'s and 2 \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s.
Together, functional-test and docker-build failures account for 46 of the
62 recorded failures (74\%).

Two related deploy-phase findings share the same underlying symptom under
different labels. \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s
\textsc{Petstore}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask} cell shows two
\texttt{unschedulable} failures (iterations 005--006, both spec-refinement):
a proposed spec passed static validation but its resources could not
actually be scheduled onto any node at apply time.
\texttt{glm-5.2}'s \textsc{ParcelPinLockerPickup}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http}
cell shows the same summary text, ``Kubernetes resources did not become
Ready within timeout'', on two consecutive spec-refinement iterations
(002--003), but recorded under a different kind, \texttt{namespace\_cleanup}.
A third occurrence of the same summary text and \texttt{unschedulable} kind
appears on \texttt{glm-5.2}'s
\textsc{ParcelPinLockerPickup}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix} cell (iteration
004, code-phase), but its diagnostic detail shows a different underlying
cause from the other two: every backend pod is \texttt{CrashLoopBackOff}
across all four worker nodes, an application-level crash, not a
resource-scheduling shortfall. That two distinct root causes
(genuine scheduling infeasibility, and an application repeatedly crashing
after it is already scheduled) surface under the same \texttt{unschedulable}
label, and that the \emph{same} symptom text appears under two different
kind labels elsewhere, means this kind field cannot be read at face value
without checking the underlying diagnostic; it is a labelling gap worth
noting for anyone extending this taxonomy, not three independent findings
about scheduling itself.

A separate, genuinely recurring deploy-phase issue shows up for two
different models: a \texttt{docker tag failed: ... No such image} error,
recorded as kind \texttt{unknown}, on \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s
\textsc{Recipes}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask} cell (iterations 005--006)
and \texttt{glm-5.2}'s \textsc{Petstore}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix} cell
(iterations 005--006). Both recover within a few iterations. Recurring
across two unrelated models and scenarios makes a harness-level
build/registry propagation race more likely than a model- or
scenario-specific cause, though this dataset cannot confirm that directly.

A positive counter-example is worth recording alongside the gaps above:
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s \textsc{TransitPulseDelayReporter}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http}
cell (iteration 001) shows static spec validation \emph{correctly}
rejecting a proposal before it was ever applied, pinning all three
database replicas onto one worker node whose combined resource request
(38{,}000m CPU) exceeded that node's allocatable budget
($\approx${}28{,}800m). A second instance of the same check firing
correctly appears on \texttt{glm-5.2}'s
\textsc{TransitPulseDelayReporter}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask} cell
(iteration 002), again a database placement pinning $32{,}000$m CPU onto
one node. This is exactly the check the
\texttt{unschedulable}/\texttt{namespace\_cleanup} cases above show gaps
in, working as designed in both instances.

The remaining kinds are small in count but each a distinct, genuine
signal: \textbf{3} \texttt{spec\_validation} failures (the two node-pinning
cases just described, plus \texttt{glm-5.2}'s
\textsc{Recipes}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix} cell), \textbf{3}
decision- or code-phase \texttt{llm\_parse} failures (all
\texttt{glm-5.2}: \textsc{Petstore}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http} at baseline,
and \textsc{SplitNestSharedExpenseLedger} on both
\textsc{Go-net-http}\,(iteration 006) and \textsc{Rust-Actix}\,(iteration
010)), and \textbf{1} \texttt{llm\_call} failure that is not a transport
fault: \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s \textsc{Petstore}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask}
cell hit its own configured \texttt{--llm-max-cost} ceiling (\$20.22 spent
against a \$20.00 cap) at iteration 010, the framework's cost-tracking
safeguard (Section~\ref{sec:methods-workflow}) doing exactly what it is
designed to do.

\paragraph{Case study: a connection-pooling bug invisible to
single-container evaluation.} \texttt{glm-5.2}'s
\textsc{Recipes}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http} baseline reaches a completed
bench but records \textbf{0} sustained goodput: the adaptive profile's
warm-up step fails health checks and explore never starts. Postgres logs
from that run show the deployment producing 953 errors during the load
window, dominated by two error classes:
\texttt{\small unnamed prepared statement does not exist} and
\texttt{\small bind message supplies N parameters, but prepared statement
requires M}. This is the classic symptom of a Go SQL driver using
server-side prepared statements against PgBouncer in \texttt{transaction}
pooling mode, where a prepared statement created on one physical
connection is invisible on the next pooled connection a later query lands
on. This bug is invisible to \textsc{BaxBench}'s original single-container
functional tests (which use a direct, unpooled connection) and only
manifests once the generated code is deployed behind the pooler this
framework introduces. Iteration~001 (code refinement) does not fix it
(goodput remains 0); iteration~002 (code refinement again, chosen freely
by the decision stage given the iteration~001 failure feedback) does,
jumping to $19{,}026.7$\,req/s. This is direct evidence that iterative
\emph{code} refinement, not deployment tuning, is the correct lever for
an infra-interaction bug the model could not have anticipated at
generation time, and that it can take more than one attempt.

\paragraph{Case study: a plausible deployment decision that backfires.}
On the same cell, iteration~003's decision stage reasons as follows
(quoted verbatim from its \texttt{decision.json}):
\begin{quote}
\small
``The code is now well-optimized (0\% failures, 19K/s goodput) and the
bottleneck is purely infrastructure: Postgres hits 200/200 connections
with PgBouncer \texttt{cl\_waiting} reaching 311, and db-primary CPU
saturates at 16.7 cores. [...] We should add database replicas, enable a
read pooler, increase Postgres \texttt{max\_connections} and PgBouncer
\texttt{default\_pool\_size}, and potentially reduce over-provisioned
backend CPU to free cluster budget for more DB resources.''
\end{quote}
The reasoning is a coherent read of the previous iteration's diagnostics
(Section~\ref{sec:methods-bench}), and the resulting spec does exactly
what it describes: database replicas 1 $\to$ 3, \texttt{max\_connections}
200 $\to$ 300, backend CPU request 2000m $\to$ 500m. The resulting
deployment, however, regresses to \textbf{0} sustained goodput. The next
iteration (004, code) recovers to $20{,}494.3$\,req/s \emph{without}
reverting the topology change, so the regression is not explained by the
added replicas alone; most plausibly the simultaneous $4\times$ backend
CPU cut left the application under-provisioned for its own request
handling while the new DB topology was still stabilising. The cell goes
on to alternate lever choices through the rest of its budget, peaking at
$24{,}477.3$\,req/s at iteration~007 before settling at $21{,}722.2$\,req/s
by iteration~010, itself not a monotonic climb, with two further
consecutive code-refinement steps (iterations~008--009) that give back
part of the gain before the final spec step recovers it.
\textbf{Lesson for the framework, not just the model}: this iteration
changed three spec fields at once, which is consistent with the
single-lever-per-iteration design (Section~\ref{sec:methods-workflow}) but
does not prevent \emph{multiple fields within one lever} from changing
simultaneously, which limits attribution within a spec-refinement step the
same way mixing code and spec changes would across steps. RQ2's finding
that \texttt{glm-5.2}'s spec-refinement mean is net-negative across 66
steps suggests this is not a one-off either for this cell or this model.

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
The evidence supports a consistent reading: essentially all \emph{genuine}
attrition happens at the code-correctness gate the agent is directly
responsible for (functional-test and docker-build failures together
account for 46 of 62 recorded failures), and the cluster-execution path is
close to, but not quite, failure-free. The two case studies together show
the same lesson from opposite directions: code refinement can fix bugs the
model could not have anticipated (the pooling case), and a single
deployment decision can undo a healthy deployment even when its diagnosis
is correct, because the framework does not constrain how many fields one
spec-refinement step may touch (the backfire case). The
\texttt{unschedulable}/\texttt{namespace\_cleanup} labelling gap is a
finding about the evaluation framework's own failure taxonomy rather than
about any model.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
\textbf{The dominant \emph{genuine} failure mode is upstream of
deployment}, in code correctness (functional-test and docker-build
failures together are 74\% of recorded failures). The cluster-execution
path is nearly, not entirely, failure-free: the
\texttt{unschedulable}/\texttt{namespace\_cleanup} cases point at a real
gap between static validation and actual scheduling feasibility, and at a
labelling inconsistency in how that gap is recorded, partially offset by
two documented cases where the same static validation correctly caught an
infeasible proposal before it was ever applied.


% ----- §5.8 Cross-Cutting Synthesis -----
\section{Cross-Cutting Synthesis}
\label{sec:results-synthesis}

Read together across the 63 cells collected, three models, and eight
scenarios, four patterns recur consistently enough to generalise beyond
any single cell:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Correctness gates deployment, consistently.} The largest
        single source of attrition (RQ6, 74\% of recorded failures) and
        the largest single-step goodput gains (RQ2) both trace back to
        code correctness, not deployment tuning. This holds across every
        model and is exactly the class of bug BaxBench's original
        single-container evaluation cannot observe
        (Section~\ref{sec:rw-benchmarks}).
  \item \textbf{Deployment refinement is real, bounded, and
        model-dependent in its downside risk.} Across every model, spec
        refinement's median per-step effect is small; its mean is
        positive for \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} and \texttt{gpt-5.5} but
        sharply negative for \texttt{glm-5.2} (RQ2), which also shows
        repeated complete regressions to zero goodput on this lever
        (RQ6), on a sample large enough (66 spec steps) that this looks
        like a genuine model-level pattern rather than noise.
  \item \textbf{This dataset does not rank the three models on completion
        reliability.} Every model reaches a working baseline and completes
        its full budget on 100\% of the cells it has data for (RQ3); the
        coverage gap that exists is concentrated almost entirely in one
        scenario, \textsc{TimeCapsuleNotesVault}, rather than spread across
        the matrix. \textsc{Python-Flask} sets a clearly lower ceiling than
        either compiled framework for every model, while the ordering
        between the two compiled frameworks is close and model-dependent
        (RQ4).
  \item \textbf{The cluster-execution path is close to, but not quite, a
        failure-free component.} Deploy-phase failures remain a small
        fraction of the total (RQ6), and the same static validation that
        occasionally misses a scheduling infeasibility also demonstrably
        catches it, twice, in the node-over-commit cases documented in
        Section~\ref{sec:results-rq6}.
\end{itemize}


% ----- §5.9 Summary -----
\section{Summary}
\label{sec:results-summary}

Across all three models and the 63 scenario/framework cells with data:
%
\begin{itemize}
  \item iterative refinement improves sustained goodput in essentially
        every cell with data, and separately rescues 27 of the 29
        \emph{dead} baselines observed into a working deployment (RQ1);
  \item code refinement contributes the largest single-step gains for
        all three models, dominated by fixes to bugs that only manifest
        under load and cluster topology; deployment refinement is
        smaller on median for all three and positive on average for two
        of three, but net-negative for \texttt{glm-5.2} (RQ2);
  \item \textbf{this dataset does not support a completion-rate ranking}:
        every cell that has data reaches baseline and completes its full
        budget; the nine cells without data are concentrated almost
        entirely in one scenario (RQ3);
  \item \textsc{Python-Flask} sets a clearly lower achievable-goodput
        ceiling than either compiled framework for all three models; the
        ordering between \textsc{Go-net-http} and \textsc{Rust-Actix} is
        close and not the same for every model (RQ4);
  \item where it converges, the agent's deployment-spec trajectory tracks
        workload characteristics sensibly, corroborated across two models
        on the same scenario (RQ5), though not every individual
        spec-refinement decision improves the outcome, even when the
        stated rationale is sound (RQ6);
  \item nearly all \emph{genuine} attrition happens at the
        code-correctness gate the agent is responsible for; the
        cluster-execution path is nearly, not entirely, failure-free, and
        the same static-validation mechanism that occasionally misses a
        scheduling infeasibility is also documented catching it on two
        separate cells (RQ6).
\end{itemize}

These findings are discussed further, including limitations and threats
to validity, in Chapter~\ref{ch:discussion}, and answered directly against
the thesis's research question in Chapter~\ref{ch:conclusion}.
